body:
Social variation in Gujarati

Language variation is not caused exclusively by geographical separation. People living in the same locality may also develop distinctive patterns of speech because of their social networks, occupations, community traditions or educational backgrounds.

A variety of language associated with a social group is called a social dialect or sociolect.

Gujarati has several historically recognised community-related speech varieties. These often exist alongside regional varieties, and an individual may share the linguistic characteristics of both.

Parsi Gujarati

The Parsi community adopted Gujarati as a major language of communication after settling in western India. Parsi Gujarati developed distinctive vocabulary and expressions influenced by Persian, the community's historical religious and cultural traditions, and later English.

Parsi Gujarati also shares features with the regional speech of southern Gujarat. The contributions of Parsi printers and journalists to Gujarati publications were particularly important during the emergence of modern print culture.

Nagari Gujarati

Nagari Gujarati is historically associated with the speech of the Nagar Brahmin community. The speech of sections of this community in central Gujarat also influenced the historical development of literary and Standard Gujarati.

The expression Nagari Gujarati in this sociolinguistic context refers to a community-associated variety of speech. It should not be confused with Nagari as the name of a writing tradition.

Other community-related varieties

Community-related speech characteristics are also found among groups such as Bohras, Khojas and Mers. These may involve distinctive expressions, specialised vocabulary and pronunciation patterns.

Such characteristics describe historically observed linguistic tendencies. They do not mean that all members of a particular community speak identically or exclusively use that community's traditional dialect.

Regional and social dialects can overlap

Regional and social dialects are not mutually exclusive categories. A person may speak a regional form of Gujarati while retaining vocabulary or expressions associated with a particular community.

A Parsi speaker from Surat may share features of Surati Gujarati with other residents of the region while also using expressions characteristic of Parsi Gujarati. In this case, geography and community identity both influence speech.

Standard language and register

Standard Gujarati is the broadly accepted form of Gujarati used in formal writing, education, dictionaries, textbooks and public communication. It has established conventions of spelling and grammar that facilitate communication across dialect regions.

A register is a form of language selected according to the situation, purpose or audience. Administrative Gujarati, literary Gujarati and everyday conversational Gujarati can differ in their choice of words and sentence structures.

For example, a person may use Kathiawadi expressions when speaking with family members and switch to Standard Gujarati when writing an official application. The difference arises from the situation and purpose of communication.

A standard language is not linguistically superior to a regional dialect. Its principal advantage is the availability of common, widely accepted conventions for formal communication.

Multilingualism and code-switching

Multilingualism refers to the use of multiple languages by an individual or a community. Gujarat's commercial history, migration and regional contacts encourage interaction among Gujarati, Hindi, English, Marathi, Sindhi and other languages.

Code-switching occurs when a speaker alternates between languages or linguistic varieties during communication. For example, a Gujarati speaker may use Gujarati while discussing family matters and switch to English while discussing technical subjects.

Code-mixing generally refers to the incorporation of words or expressions from one language into communication primarily conducted in another language.

These practices demonstrate the ability of speakers to adapt their language to different audiences and circumstances.

Vocabulary and language contact

Gujarati vocabulary contains words inherited through its Indo-Aryan linguistic history as well as words adopted from other languages.

  • Tatsama: Words adopted from Sanskrit with little modification in their form.
  • Tadbhava: Words derived historically from earlier Indo-Aryan forms through successive changes in pronunciation or structure.
  • Deshaja: Indigenous or locally developed words whose derivation is not straightforwardly traced to Sanskrit.
  • Loanwords: Words adopted through contact with other languages, including Persian, Arabic, Portuguese and English.

Examples of borrowed vocabulary used in Gujarati include darvajo, associated with Persian and meaning door, kitab, of Arabic origin and meaning book, and batata, meaning potato, ultimately associated with Portuguese.

The historical presence of Persian in administration, the maritime trade of western India and the expansion of English-medium education contributed to different layers of borrowed vocabulary.

Borrowing words from another language does not change the basic genealogical classification of Gujarati. Gujarati remains an Indo-Aryan language despite its extensive linguistic contacts.

Prelims focus

  • A sociolect is a socially associated language variety.
  • Parsi Gujarati and Nagari Gujarati illustrate community-related variation.
  • Standard Gujarati is widely used in formal writing and education.
  • Register depends on the purpose, audience and situation of communication.
  • Tatsama and Tadbhava describe different historical relationships with earlier Indo-Aryan vocabulary.
  • Trap: A speaker can use a regional dialect, a community-related variety and Standard Gujarati in different contexts.

[References: Central Institute of Indian Languages, Compendium of Linguistic Resources in Indian Languages, edited by Narayan Choudhary, 2021, Gujarati Raw Speech Corpus section; The Written Languages of the World: A Survey of the Degree and Modes of Use, Vol. 2, India, Book 1, Registrar General and Census Commissioner, India, 1989, Gujarati section; Encyclopaedia Iranica, Gujarati, Vol. XI, Fascicle 4, pp. 391–392; Gujarati Vishwakosh, Gujarat: Gujarati Language and Literature, sections on community dialects and vocabulary; NCERT, Our Pasts II, Class 7, 2020–21 edition, Chapter 9, The Making of Regional Cultures, pp. 122 and 130–131. Online sources consulted on 26 November 2026.]

title: Social Dialects, Standard Gujarati and Language Contact

body:
Constitutional recognition of Gujarati

Gujarati is included in the Eighth Schedule of the Constitution of India. It was among the original 14 languages included when the Constitution came into force in 1950.

Following subsequent constitutional amendments, the Eighth Schedule contains 22 languages. Its provisions are associated with Article 344(1), concerning the Official Language Commission, and Article 351, concerning the development of Hindi.

Inclusion in the Eighth Schedule gives a language constitutional recognition. It does not automatically make that language the official language of the Union or of every Indian state.

Official language status in Gujarat

The Gujarat Official Languages Act, 1960, identified as Gujarat Act No. 1 of 1961 and dated 15 February 1961, provides the statutory basis for the official languages of Gujarat.

Section 2 provides for Hindi written in Devanagari script and Gujarati to be used for the state's official purposes. The State Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, exclude specified purposes or restrict Hindi to specified official purposes.

The Act illustrates the difference between the widespread use of a regional language, its recognition under the Constitution and its designation for official government functions.

The Eighth Schedule recognises languages at the constitutional level. The Gujarat Official Languages Act provides for languages used for the official purposes of the State of Gujarat. These are different forms of recognition.

Gujarati in the population census

The Census of India records the mother tongues reported by individuals and presents them under language categories.

According to Census 2011, the Gujarati language category accounted for 55,492,554 mother-tongue speakers in India, representing approximately 4.58% of the country's population. Gujarati ranked 6th among the scheduled languages by reported mother-tongue population in that enumeration.

These figures relate specifically to the 2011 Census and were reproduced in the Government of India's answer to Lok Sabha Unstarred Question No. 364 on 20 July 2021. They are historical census figures, not estimates of the Gujarati-speaking population in 2026.

Mother-tongue population also differs from the total number of people who can speak Gujarati. A person whose mother tongue is another language may learn and use Gujarati as an additional language.

Gujarati beyond Gujarat

Gujarati-speaking communities are also found in Maharashtra, particularly Mumbai, as well as outside India. Historical trading networks and migration contributed to the spread of Gujarati to East Africa, the United Kingdom, North America and other regions.

Gujarati used by overseas communities can acquire vocabulary and expressions from the languages of their adopted countries. Such changes illustrate the continuing development of Gujarati through multilingual contact.

Distinguishing the essential concepts

ConceptMeaningGujarati example
Language familyLanguages sharing historical ancestryIndo-European
Language branchA subgroup within a language familyIndo-Aryan
Historical stageA period in a language's developmentOld Gujarati
ScriptSystem of written representationGujarati script
Regional dialectGeographically associated speech varietyPattani
Social dialectSocially associated speech varietyParsi Gujarati
RegisterUsage adapted to a situationAdministrative Gujarati
Standard languageForm used in common formal communicationStandard Gujarati
Scheduled languageLanguage listed in the Eighth ScheduleGujarati

The same language can be studied from all these perspectives. Gujarati has a historical ancestry, a distinctive script, regional and social varieties, a standard written form and constitutional recognition. Each characteristic answers a different question about the language.

Prelims focus

  • Gujarati was among the original 14 languages of the Eighth Schedule.
  • The Eighth Schedule contains 22 languages.
  • The Gujarat Official Languages Act is titled as an Act of 1960 but is Gujarat Act No. 1 of 1961.
  • Section 2 provides for Hindi in Devanagari script and Gujarati, subject to notified exceptions and specifications.
  • Census 2011 recorded Gujarati at approximately 4.58% of India's population by mother tongue.
  • Trap: Mother tongue, official language, scheduled language and total speaker population are distinct concepts.

[References: Constitution of India, Eighth Schedule, Articles 344(1) and 351, Legislative Department edition; Government of Gujarat, Gujarat Official Languages Act, 1960, Gujarat Act No. 1 of 1961, Sections 1–2, official India Code text modified up to 31 October 2012; Government of India, Lok Sabha Unstarred Question No. 364, answered 20 July 2021, annexure containing Census 2011 scheduled-language population figures; Encyclopaedia Iranica, Gujarati, Vol. XI, Fascicle 4, pp. 391–392; Central Institute of Indian Languages, Gujarati Raw Speech Corpus, regional dialect classification. Constitutional and statutory references consulted on 26 November 2026; population figures refer to Census 2011.]
